title: Josh Hart ‘not in a good headspace’ as Knicks wing’s early slump continues
content:
INDIANAPOLIS — Josh Hart is searching for answers.

The New York Knicks’ sparkplug wing is “not in a good headspace,” he said Friday, after the team’s 106-104 loss to the Indiana Pacers.

“Just have to be better,” Hart said. “Have to be better mentally. I just gotta get my mental right.”

Hart missed all four of his field goal attempts and failed to score. It was his second game back from a weeklong absence, which was due to ankle soreness and then an illness. Just as notably, this was not Hart’s first time struggling this season.

The 31-year-old has spent most of the Knicks’ first 12 games this season in a slump. Friday’s game was his sixth consecutive performance with fewer than 10 points. He is shooting 36 percent from the field this season. Head coach Mike Brown kept him on the bench for the entire fourth quarter in Indiana.

As for how Hart can “get (his) mental right”?

“Wish I could tell you,” he said. “Don’t know. … I gotta figure out how to improve that and improve my play.”

He opted not to go further in depth.

Hart is hardly the only Knicks wing in his feelings right now. Fresh off a championship, the trio that he nicknamed “Wingstop,” made up of Hart, Mikal Bridges and OG Anunoby, has struggled this autumn.

Bridges was one of the NBA’s coldest shooters coming into Friday night, shooting 33 percent from the field and 27 percent from 3-point range, but he bounced back against Indiana. Early in the game, he hit a midrange shot, scored on a cut and then rolled in a layup. The first-quarter buckets got him going. He finished with 18 points on 8-of-12 shooting against the Pacers, though a return to normal was not enough for the Knicks to walk away victorious.

Anunoby has been uncharacteristic, too. Normally a burly attacker of the rim, his drives into the paint have been chaotic. He was shooting just 58 percent at the basket coming into Friday. For perspective, his career average is 70 percent. The jumper has been errant, too, and the funk continued into the Pacers game, when Anunoby scored 11 points on 4-of-13 shooting.

When asked why he’s erred around the rim more to begin this season, Anunoby, a man of few words, responded with two.

“Not sure,” he said.

Hart has theories for his own slow start. The ankle injury that kept him out of two games last week occurred in training camp, he said. He had dealt with it throughout the beginning of the season. He also revealed that he tweaked a calf in September, an ailment that kept him off the court for three weeks leading into the preseason. Once he returned to the court, he was limited during practices.

The loss to the Pacers dropped New York to 6-6, below where it expected to be after a dozen games. The Knicks have lost close games. Each defeat has been by single digits. Karl-Anthony Towns is off to a raucous start. The reserves, especially Landry Shamet and Miles “Deuce” McBride, are contributing.

But the Knicks are missing shots.

They are focused on speeding up the offense, which is moving at a glacial pace at times. Getting into transition more could help the group’s percentages around the hoop, considering that a well-run fast break often ends in a layup.

Each of the three starting wings is shooting worse than 40 percent from the field. Hart is looking for mental clarity. Bridges is searching for more baskets. And Anunoby is just playing the waiting game.

“It’s early,” Anunoby said. “We’re not where we wanna be, but it’s November. Everything needs to be better.”
